title: De transformatione serierum in fractiones continuas, ubi simul haec theoria non mediocriter amplificatur

deep.reconstruction:
This page (printed pp. 174–175) finishes the worked examples of the series-to-continued-fraction method of §§56–58 and introduces the shift theorem of §62.

Setting from §58. Take Z = ∫dz/√(1+z²) = arsinh z (Euler writes l(z+√(1+zz))). Put z² = x/y. Then
V = √x/√(x+y) · l((√x+√(x+y))/√y) = Σ_{n≥0} (−1)^n [2·4···2n / (3·5···(2n+1))] (x/y)^{n+1}.
This is the series of arsinh(z)/(z√(1+z²)) times z², a ₂F₁(1,1;3/2;−z²)-type series. Its term ratio is rational, so Euler's general theorem gives
√(x(x+y)) / l((√x+√(x+y))/√y) = y + 1·2xy/(3y−2x + 3·4xy/(5y−4x + 5·6xy/(7y−6x + …))).

§59, x = y = 1:
- Continued fraction: √2/l(1+√2) = 1 + 1·2/(1 + 3·4/(1 + 5·6/(1+…))). All partial denominators equal 1.
- Series: l(1+√2)/√2 = 1 − 2/3 + 2·4/(3·5) − ….

§59, x = 1, y = 2:
- Series: 1/2 − (2/3)(1/4) + (2·4/(3·5))(1/8) − … = l((1+√3)/√2)/√3.
- Continued fraction: √3/l((1+√3)/√2) = 2 + 1·2·2/(4 + 3·4·2/(6 + 5·6·2/(8+…))).
- Halving and applying an equivalence transformation gives √3/(2 l((1+√3)/√2)) = 1 + 1/(2 + 6/(3 + 15/(4 + 28/(5+…)))). The k-th numerator is (2k−1)(2k)·2/4 = (2k−1)k = T_{2k−1}, i.e. 'triangular numbers taken alternately'.

§60, x = 1, y = 3. The radicals disappear because (1+2)/√3 = √3:
- Series: ¼ l3 = 1/3 − (2/3)(1/9) + (2·4/(3·5))(1/27) − ….
- Continued fraction: 4/l3 = 3 + 1·2·3/(7 + 3·4·3/(11 + 5·6·3/(15 + 7·8·3/(19+…)))).

§61. Euler claims he has opened 'a quite new method' of turning arbitrary series into continued fractions. He recalls the §42 passage from 1/(1+1/(2+2/(3+…))) = 1/(e−1) to 1+1/(2+2/(3+…)) = e/(e−1).

§62 (next page). He generalizes that passage as a shift theorem. If s = aA/(αA + bB/(βB + …)), then t = bs/(a−αs) = βA + cA/(γB + dB/(δC + …)). This is proved by equivalence transformations and by inverting s = at/(αt+b).
errors: No errors found. Numerical checks: √2/l(1+√2) ≈ 1.6045; √3/(2 l((1+√3)/√2)) ≈ 1.3151, with convergent ≈ 1.302 at depth 5; 4/l3 ≈ 3.641, with convergent ≈ 3.636. All formulas, including the triangular-number numerators, are correct.

Gap: for x = y = 1 the series 1 − 2/3 + 8/15 − … converges only conditionally, since its terms decay like n^{-1/2}. Its sum is justified by Abel's theorem. The continued fraction 1 + 2/(1 + 12/(1 + 30/…)) converges slowly and oscillates. Euler does not discuss convergence.
Euler leaves l((1+√3)/√2) unsimplified; it equals ½ l(2+√3).

ideas.what: Applying the series-to-CF theorem to the arsinh/log series to get continued fractions for √2/ln(1+√2), √3/ln((1+√3)/√2) and 4/ln3
ideas.modern_name: Euler-type continued fraction for a hypergeometric series ₂F₁(1,1;3/2;−z²) (arcsin/arsinh divided by √(1±z²))
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Euler's continued fraction formula); later Gauss continued fraction for ratios of ₂F₁
ideas.where_published: E593 itself (Opera postuma / Opuscula analytica II); similar log/arctan continued fractions appear in E71 and E123

ideas.what: Equivalence transformation turning numerators (2k−1)(2k)·2 into the odd triangular numbers 1, 6, 15, 28, …
Shift theorem: if s = a/(α + b/t) then t = bs/(a−αs), generalizing 1/(e−1) → e/(e−1)
ideas.modern_name: tail/shift relation of continued fractions (Möbius inversion of the first linear fractional map)

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine specializations of Euler's general series-to-CF theorem, and the shift theorem is elementary algebra. The continued fractions for ln3 and ln(1+√2) are equivalent to classical Euler/Gauss-type expansions. Nothing appears missing from the record.
